The Microscopic World of Cells

  • Organisms are either single-celled, such as most prokaryotes and protists, or multicellular, such as plants, animals, and most fungi.
  • Cell theory states that all living things are composed of cells and that all cells come from earlier cells.
  • Every cell in your body (and in every other living organism on Earth) was formed by division of a previously living cell.

Size Ranges

Text description of this image

Objects about half a millimeter in size and larger are visible with the naked eye. Objects between 1 millimeter and about 100 nanometer can be viewed through light microscope. Objects between 100 micrometer and about 1 nanometer can be viewed through electron microscope. The size scale along with examples is as follows:

10 meters to 1 meter - Human height (about 2 meters); 1 meter to 10 centimeters - Length of some nerve and muscle cells (about 0.8 meters); 10 centimeters to 1 centimeter - Chicken egg (about 7 centimeters); 1 centimeter to 1 millimeter - Frog eggs (about 2 millimeters); 1 millimeter to 100 micrometers - Paramecium; 100 micrometers to 10 micrometers - Plant and animal cells; 10 micrometers to 1 micrometer – Nucleus (about 8 micrometers); most bacteria; mitochondria (about 2 micrometers); 1 micrometer to 100 nanometers - Smallest bacteria (about 100 nanometers); 100 nanometers to 10 nanometers - Viruses (about 70 to 100 nanometers); Ribosomes (about 20 nanometers); 10 nanometers to 1 nanometer - Proteins (about 5 to 10 nanometers); lipids (about 2 to 5 nanometers); 1 nanometer to 0.1 nanometers - Small molecules (about 0.5 to 1 nanometers); atoms (about 0.1 nanometers)

The Two Major Categories of Cells

  • Biologists classify all life into three major groups called domains.
    • Organisms of the domains Bacteria and Archaea are composed of prokaryotic cells.
    • Organisms of the domain Eukarya—including protists, plants, fungi, and animals—are composed of eukaryotic cells.
Text description of this image

A table illustrates the comparison between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. The details of the prokaryotic cells depicted in the table are as follows: An image shows a prokaryotic cell.

First evolved approximately 3.5 billion years ago; Found in bacteria and archaea; Smaller, simpler; Most have cell walls; some have capsules, fimbriae, and/or flagella.; Have a plasma membrane; No membrane-bound organelles; Have a nucleoid region containing a single circular chromosome; Have ribosomes

The details of the prokaryotic cells depicted in the table are as follows: An image shows a eukaryotic cell.

First evolved approximately 2.1 billion years ago; Found in protists, plants, fungi, and animals; Larger, more complex; Plant cells have cell walls; animal cells are surrounded by an extracellular matrix.; Have a plasma membrane; Membrane-bound organelles (for example, nucleus, ER); Have a nucleus containing one or more linear chromosomes; Have ribosomes.

A Prokaryotic Cell

Text description of this image

Figure a shows A colorized transmission electron micrograph at a magnification of 18,700 shows a rod-shaped prokaryotic cell with long, whip-like extensions protruding from one end. Figure b shows the rod-shaped cell surrounded by a capsule, a sticky coating. Numerous short hair-like fimbriae (attachment structures) can be seen extending from the cell. Beneath the capsule is the cell wall that provides rigidity. The plasma membrane can be seen enclosing the cytoplasm. Several ribosome that synthesize proteins can be seen in the cytoplasm. The long extensions coming out of one end are the flagella used for propulsion.

An Idealized Animal Cell and Plant Cell

Text description of this image

figure a shows The internal structures of an animal cell reveal a plasma membrane surrounding the cell.; Cytoskeleton is shown as cable-like structures that branch throughout the interior of the cell.; Ribosomes are small structures scattered throughout the cytoplasm and studding the rough ER.; Centrosome is a small star-shaped structure, while lysosome is a spherical, bubble-like structure.; The nucleus is a large, prominent structure, surrounded by the ER.; The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (ER) forms a network of membranes and sacs with a smooth surface.; The Golgi apparatus is a large, membranous structure composed of many layers.; The rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a layered structure surrounding the nucleus and is studded with ribosomes.; The mitochondria are kidney-bean shaped structures with inner membranous folds. and The figure b shows an idealized plant cell with straight edges.; The internal structures of plant cell reveals a cell wall, which is a rigid outer cell structure surrounding the plasma membrane, surrounding the cell.; Cytoskeleton is shown as cable-like structures that branch throughout the interior of the cell.; Ribosomes are small structures scattered throughout the cytoplasm and studding the rough ER.; The nucleus is large, prominent structure, surrounded by the ER.; The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (ER) forms a network of membranes and sacs with a smooth surface.; The Golgi apparatus is a large, membranous structure composed of many layers.; The rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a layered structure surrounding the nucleus and is studded with ribosomes.; The mitochondria are kidney-bean shaped structures with inner membranous folds.; Central vacuole is a large sac-like structure that comprises about a third of the interior of the cell.; Chloroplasts are structures containing stacks of green discs.; Channels can be seen between cells as openings in the cell wall.

Membrane Structure

  • The plasma membrane separates the living cell from its nonliving surroundings.
  • The plasma membrane and other membranes of the cell are composed mostly of phospholipids, arranged into a two-layer sheet called a phospholipid bilayer.
  • The plasma membrane is a fluid mosaic:
    • fluid because molecules can move freely past one another and
    • a mosaic because of the diversity of proteins in the membrane.
Text description of this image

The figure a shows two phospholipid layers arranged such that only the heads face both the fluid on the outside of the cell and the cytoplasm inside the cell, while the ends of the tails of both layers point toward each other inside the membrane and The figure b shows the phospholipid bilayer with interspersed proteins that span the bilayer, with hydrophilic regions contacting the outside of the cell and hydrophobic regions contacting the interior of the membrane with the hydrophobic phospholipid tails.

Cell Surfaces

  • Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose fibers.
  • Plant cell walls protect the cells, maintain cell shape, and keep cells from absorbing too much water.
  • Animal cells lack cell walls and most secrete a sticky coat called the extracellular matrix.
  • The surfaces of most animal cells contain cell junctions, structures that connect cells together into tissues, allowing the cells to function in a coordinated way.

The Nucleus and Ribosomes: Genetic Control of the Cell

  • The nucleus is the control center of the cell.
    • Each gene is a stretch of DNA that stores the information necessary to produce a protein.
    • Proteins do most of the actual work of the cell.
  • The nucleus is separated from the cytoplasm by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope.
  • The nucleolus is
    • a prominent structure within the nucleus and
    • the site where the components of ribosomes are made.
Text description of this image

The figure a shows the nucleus with a large spherical structure that contains the chromatin fibers and the prominent nucleolus. The nuclear envelope, covered with openings called nuclear pores, surrounds the nucleus. The membranous folds surrounding the nucleus are drawn studded with small ribosomes and figure b shows The first micrograph of the surface of the nuclear envelope at a magnification of 8,800 resembles the moon covered with what appear as small bumps. These are the nuclear pores. The second micrograph of the nuclear pores at a magnification of 12,500 shows star-like clusters of openings on the nuclear envelope.

Ribosomes

  • Ribosomes are responsible for protein synthesis.
  • In eukaryotic cells, components of ribosomes are
    • made in the nucleus and then
    • transported through the pores of the nuclear envelope into the cytoplasm, where ribosomes begin their work.
  • Some ribosomes make proteins that remain within the cytosol.
  • Other ribosomes make proteins that are incorporated into membranes or secreted by the cell.
Text description of this image

A figure shows two subunits of a ribosome with a single-stranded mRNA molecule between the two. A protein resembling beads of a string can be seen protruding from one end.

The Endomembrane System: Manufacturing and Distributing Cellular Products

  • The endomembrane system in a cell consists of
    • the nuclear envelope,
    • the endoplasmic reticulum (ER),
    • the Golgi apparatus,
    • lysosomes, and
    • vacuoles.
  • These membranous organelles are either physically connected or linked by vesicles, sacs made of membrane.

Chloroplasts and Mitochondria: Providing Cellular Energy

  • One of the central themes of biology is the transformation of energy: how it enters living systems, is converted from one form to another, and is eventually given off as heat.
  • Two organelles act as cellular power stations:
    • chloroplasts and
    • mitochondria.

The Cytoskeleton: Cell Shape and Movement

  • The cytoskeleton
    • is a network of protein fibers extending throughout the cytoplasm and
    • serves as both skeleton and “muscles” for the cell, functioning in support and movement.
  • The cytoskeleton
    • provides mechanical support to the cell and
    • helps a cell maintain its shape.
